verified_metadata.title: Towards Best Practice in Explaining Neural Network Decisions with LRP
verified_metadata.venue: 2020 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)

metadata_sources.supports: Official author record confirms title, ordered authors, seven-page v3 and IJCNN 2020 presentation.
IEEE-deposited DOI record confirms proceedings venue, publisher, 2020 year and pages 1–7; IEEE landing page itself required JavaScript.
Author-hosted earlier manuscript confirms title and author identity; the later arXiv v3 was also downloaded and used for content checks.

artifact.version_note: Seven-page arXiv v3 dated 13 July 2020, described by authors as presented at IJCNN 2020. Title and ordered authors read directly. Earlier five-page author manuscript preserved as Kohlbrenner2020.pdf.

contexts.evidence: Sections II-A/B (pp.2–3) contrast uniform redistribution with composites using epsilon/z, alpha-beta, and flat rules, addressing gradient shattering and class discriminativity.
Section II-B (p.3) describes the layer-dependent best practice and Section IV compares resulting attribution quality. This supports the overview/best-practice citation.
Section III-C, Eq.(5), p.4 defines inside-total positive relevance with ground-truth boxes; Section IV-A compares LRP composites using this measure. The thesis expressly changes boxes to masks.

Section III-C, Eq.(5), p.4 sums positive relevance, whereas the thesis preceding definition uses absolute attributions (abs=true). The formula is a reasonable adaptation but differs in both sign treatment and object annotation.
contexts.proposed_replacement: \paragraph{Attribution localization (AL).} Adapted from the inside-total relevance ratio of~\textcite{Kohlbrenner2020}, who sum positive relevance within ground-truth bounding boxes; we use absolute attribution mass and ImageNet-S pixel masks:

contexts.evidence: Sections III-C and IV-A (p.4) compare rule choices by object-localization ratios. This supports the stated precedent; the thesis separately acknowledges that localization is not faithfulness.
Sections II-B and IV-A (pp.3–4) use epsilon/z, alpha-beta, and flat composites, and do not introduce or compare an LRP-gamma rule.

notes: Existing abbreviated venue IJCNN is correct. DOI and expanded venue above can be added as optional metadata enrichment.

verified_metadata.title: Explaining nonlinear classification decisions with deep Taylor decomposition

metadata_sources.supports: Publisher record verifies ordered published author list, title, Pattern Recognition 65, May 2017, pp.211–222 and DOI.
German National Library copy of the CC-BY published article confirms exact journal metadata and full text.
Author manuscript independently confirms title/authors and relevant mathematical construction.

artifact.version_note: Published CC-BY journal version, 12 pages, printed pp.211–222; title/authors and DOI read on first page. Author manuscript is preserved as Montavon2017DeepTaylor.pdf.

contexts.evidence: Sections 2–5 introduce attribution by decomposition and propagate relevance through a neural network. Correct background citation to Deep Taylor decomposition.

Section 4.2 (p.216) derives z+ and identifies alpha=1,beta=0 on positive inputs. Neither the published paper nor the author manuscript states the claimed explicit open problem about the general alpha-beta rule; the conclusion on p.220 does not make that statement.
contexts.proposed_replacement: Deep Taylor~\parencite{Montavon2017DeepTaylor} justifies the $z^+$-rule for positive input spaces. Our \ac{rg} supplies a game-theoretic construction for the generalized $\alpha\beta$ rule.

contexts.evidence: Section 4.2 (p.216) identifies the z+ rule with alpha=1,beta=0 for positive input spaces, without epsilon stabilization. Section 6.2 (p.218) discusses nonnegative-bias handling. The exact identification should state the activation and epsilon conditions.
contexts.proposed_replacement: For nonnegative activations and $\varepsilon=0$, $(\alpha,\beta)=(1,0)$ gives the $z^+$-rule of Deep Taylor decomposition~\parencite{Montavon2017DeepTaylor}, with bias absorption as above; positive $\varepsilon$ gives its stabilized variant.

contexts.evidence: Sections 2–5 and the image experiments establish Deep Taylor as a backward attribution family for neural classifiers. This supports the relevant background list, without independently validating the thesis’s new split-pair claim.

notes: Metadata content is correct; proposed BibTeX only normalizes the DOI field to the bare identifier and page-range syntax.
The original arXiv record lists Sebastian Bach; the published paper and author manuscript list Sebastian Lapuschkin. The thesis correctly cites the published author list.

verified_metadata.title: Methods for interpreting and understanding deep neural networks

metadata_sources.supports: Publisher record confirms title, author biographies/order, Digital Signal Processing 73, February 2018, pp.1–15 and DOI.
Author-hosted full tutorial verifies ordered authors and content, including LRP and explanation selectivity.

artifact.version_note: Author manuscript with 14 PDF pages, corresponding to the 2018 journal article with published pages 1–15; title and three authors verified. Evidence page numbers below refer to this manuscript.

contexts.evidence: Sections 4–5 review neural explanations and LRP/Deep Taylor, supporting the cited attribution-family overview.
Section 5, especially p.6 Eq.(1), explains redistribution/conservation and alpha-beta LRP, while Section 6 gives practical recommendations. The gamma rule is attributed separately in the thesis.

Section 7.2 (p.10) defines selectivity by deleting high-relevance features/patches and taking area under the remaining function-value curve, with lower AUC preferred. The manuscript example uses 4-by-4 black patches; the thesis explicitly specifies its own 39-by-39 mean-replacement/Quantus implementation.

notes: Metadata content is correct; proposed BibTeX normalizes the DOI field and page-range syntax.

verified_metadata.title: Monotone and Partially Monotone Neural Networks

metadata_sources.supports: Author institutional record confirms title, authors, journal, year, volume 21, issue 6, pages 906–917 and DOI.
Indexed original abstract confirms full author names and bibliographic details; online publication 5 April 2010, June 2010 issue.
Institutional repository confirms the original abstract on parameter constraints and positive-weight theory; bibliographic record has no full-text download.

artifact.version_note: No accessible full paper found through publisher, Erasmus repository, Tilburg author/institution searches, or Radboud group publication list. Institutional metadata/abstract page saved separately as Daniels2010_MonotoneNN.abstract.html; it is not full text.

contexts.evidence: The public abstract explicitly discusses monotone neural networks obtained by parameter constraints, positive-weight theory, and partially monotone extensions of Sill min–max networks. This supports the cited background on monotonic networks; the broader interpretability framing is the thesis author’s synthesis. Full text was unavailable.

The public abstract supports weight constraints as a method for monotone neural networks, but does not establish the historical superlative “oldest” or priority among all monotone models. Full text was unavailable, so no claim is made about unseen historical discussion.
contexts.proposed_replacement: Weight-sign constraints are a classical device for building monotone neural networks \parencite{Sill1997_MonotonicNetworks,Daniels2010_MonotoneNN} and remain the structural core of modern certified-monotone architectures \parencite{Liu2020CertifiedMonotone,Runje_2023}.

notes: Metadata is verified; full-text content and identity could not be verified. The current abbreviated journal name denotes the correct journal, though the full name would improve consistency.

verified_metadata.title: Analyzing Multi-Head Self-Attention: Specialized Heads Do the Heavy Lifting, the Rest Can Be Pruned
verified_metadata.venue: Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics

metadata_sources.supports: Official proceedings entry confirms exact title, ordered authors, ACL 2019, pp.5797–5808 and DOI.

artifact.version_note: Final ACL 2019 proceedings PDF, pp.5797–5808; title/authors and conference footer verified.

contexts.evidence: Sections 4–5 (pp.5798–5801) rank encoder heads using LRP and characterize their roles; Section 6 connects these findings with pruning. This supports attribution-based head identification.

Section 4 (pp.5798–5799) evaluates heads using both attention confidence and LRP contribution to the predicted logit. Section 5 inspects attention patterns and Section 6 validates with pruning. Describing this paper as reading only the attention weights directly as explanations omits its central attribution analysis.
contexts.proposed_replacement: Early analyses of head roles and pruning combined attention patterns with LRP-based importance estimates and pruning experiments~\parencite{Voita2019}.

contexts.evidence: Preprint §4.1–4.3, especially Theorem 4.5 (p. 8) and the piecewise-affine characterization on p. 9, proves that networks built from affine layers and piecewise-affine activations such as ReLU form affine spline operators.
